bullets: How tables, balance points and bell curves turn chance into exact answers: distributions, binomial, normal and independence
slides.heading: JC H2 probability: distributions, binomial, normal, independence
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build probability from the ground up - a table that must add to 1, an expectation that balances a distribution, a binomial count of successes, a normal curve pinned by its mean and spread - and by the end you will know why a coin never remembers.

bullets: Check and use a discrete probability distribution such as X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, whose expectation is 1.1
Use the binomial formula and the normal 68-95-99.7 rule: P(X = 3) for n = 10, p = 0.3 is about 0.267, and about 95% of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about a run of heads making tails due.

bullets: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row, and most people feel the next toss should be tails
The sixth toss does not know about the first five - so is the feeling right, or is it a trap?
slides.heading: Five heads in a row - is tails now more likely?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any formulas: heads, tails, or exactly even? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because independence is the last idea of the lesson and it settles this question completely.

bullets: A discrete probability distribution lists every outcome with its probability, and the probabilities always sum to 1
Expectation is the probability-weighted average: E(X) = sum of x times P(X = x), the long-run mean of the distribution
The binomial counts successes in independent trials, and the normal curve is described completely by its mean and standard deviation
slides.heading: One subject, four tools: tables, averages, counts, curves
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: every model in this topic is a way of spreading total probability 1 across outcomes - the only question is whether the spread sits in a table, a count, or a smooth curve.

bullets: X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, and the chips travel into the sum: 0.2 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 1
Something has to happen, so every discrete distribution's probabilities sum to exactly 1 - check every table first
slides.heading: A probability table must add to 1
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the three probability chips travel into the sum and land on exactly 1 - if a table ever sums to anything else, the table is wrong before any question begins.

bullets: E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1: each value weighted by its probability
The probe slides along the axis and the fulcrum rises at 1.1: the whole distribution balances exactly at its expectation
slides.heading: Expectation: the balance point
slides.notes: Stress the balance picture: expectation is not the most likely value - X is never 1.1 - it is the centre of mass of the distribution and the long-run average over many repeats.

bullets: Exactly 3 successes in 10 trials means choosing which 3 trials succeed: 10 choose 3 is 120 ways
Each path has probability 0.3^3 times 0.7^7, so P(X = 3) = 120 times that, about 0.267
slides.heading: Binomial: n = 10, p = 0.3
slides.notes: Work the formula in two beats: first count the arrangements with the binomial coefficient, then multiply by the probability of one arrangement - successes at 0.3 each, failures at 0.7 each. Never forget either half.

bullets: About 68% of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two, about 99.7% within three
Watch the shaded band widen from one sigma to three while the test marker slides into the tail: almost nothing lies beyond three sigma
slides.heading: The 68–95–99.7 rule
slides.notes: Point at the widening band and say: the rule turns a mean and a standard deviation into instant probability estimates - no table needed for these three landmarks.

bullets: The trap claim is: After five heads in a row, tails is due.
Independent tosses have no memory: the memory needle never moves, and after five heads the next toss is still 1/2 heads and 1/2 tails
slides.heading: A common mistake: tails is due after five heads
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: a run of five heads has probability 1/32 before it starts, but once it has happened it changes nothing about the next toss.

bullets: Step 1: check the table: 0.2 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 1, so the distribution is valid
Step 2: weight each value by its probability: E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1
slides.heading: Worked example: expectation of the s1 distribution
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: the sum check comes first every time, because an expectation computed from a table that does not add to 1 is meaningless.

bullets: For n = 10, p = 0.3, write down P(X = 3) using the binomial coefficient 120 and the path probability 0.3^3 times 0.7^7
Careful - a classmate looks at five heads in a row and says: After five heads in a row, tails is due. Explain to them why the next toss is still 1/2
slides.heading: Your turn: compute, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the two halves of the binomial formula first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the due-tails trap.

bullets: On your own: check that the distribution 0.2, 0.5, 0.3 sums to 1 and compute its expectation
Watch out for the trap one last time: After five heads in a row, tails is due. Say what the probability of tails on the next toss really is
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for a clean expectation calculation in your first answer and one clear sentence about independence in your second.
